# Fitts's Law

Paul Fitts, 1954. The time to point at a target depends on how far away it is and how big it is,
logarithmically:

```
MT = a + b · log₂(2D / W)
```

`D` is the distance to the target, `W` its width along the axis of movement, and `a` and `b` are
fitted constants for the device and the person.

## Two consequences worth more than the formula

**Doubling the width buys the same as halving the distance.** Both change `D/W` by a factor of
two, so both save `b` milliseconds. Layout arguments about proximity and arguments about size
are the same argument, and they can be traded against each other quantitatively.

**A target at a screen edge is effectively infinitely wide.** The pointer cannot overshoot past
the edge, so `W` in the direction of travel is unbounded and the log term collapses. That is why
menu bars sit flush against edges and corners, and why a one-pixel gap below a bar destroys the
advantage completely — the target stops being an edge target and becomes an ordinary one.

The edge case *is* the design. This is the same shape of reasoning as the boundary conditions
that carry the weight in [[computer-arithmetic-and-number-representation]] — the p's complement
of zero, the most negative two's-complement value, the smallest subnormal. Interesting behaviour
lives at the limits of the range.

## Why this is in the wiki and the Gestalt principles are not

Fitts's Law makes a numeric prediction about a specific interface, so it can be **wrong** about
that interface, and being wrong is checkable. "Apply the principle of closure" cannot be wrong
about anything.

Both belong in a human-computer interaction course and only one belongs in a test suite. Knowing
which is which is the transferable skill, and it generalises well past interface design: the
same distinction separates [[counted-complexity-assertions]] from a docstring claiming an
algorithm is fast.

## The limit of the law

It predicts *pointing* time. It says nothing about whether the user knew which target to point
at, whether the target was the right one to offer, or whether the task should have existed. A
layout optimised purely on Fitts's Law can be measurably fast and useless.

That boundary is why the concept sits at `confidence: medium` and why no repository was built
from it: a formula is not an artefact, and the assessed half of the course — heuristic
evaluation — is a rubric applied by a person, which rebuilds into a form rather than a program.

## Source

The archive's HCI material teaches it with the equation rather than as a slogan, and works the
edge-target argument through real sites. Recorded in [[pwr-subject-notes]]; the folder produced
no repository and the reason is written down there rather than left implicit.
